overview: The biblical books of Samuel and Kings describe David and Solomon ruling from Jerusalem. The scale, political organization and archaeological traces of a united monarchy in the tenth century BCE remain debated. The imported map’s 1500-500 BCE span and enormous fixed outline are not evidence for that kingdom’s lifespan or borders. This card separates the biblical narrative, dated regional discoveries and clearly labelled evidence from the later kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

periods.title: The tenth-century question
periods.summary: This approximate interval frames the traditional setting of David and Solomon. Archaeological dates and political interpretations require separate assessment.

periods.title: Later kingdoms and material evidence
periods.summary: Israel and Judah developed distinct political histories. Ninth-century inscriptions and later buildings provide evidence from these subsequent societies.

periods.title: Conquest, exile and continuing communities
periods.summary: Babylonian conquest ended Judah’s monarchy, while communities continued in the homeland and abroad under later imperial rule.

sections.title: A famous story and a difficult historical question

items.text: In 2 Samuel 5, representatives of Israel meet David at Hebron, acknowledge him as king and enter an agreement with him. The story then makes Jerusalem his royal centre. It presents kingship through relationships with elders, warfare and divine support. This is the biblical account, not a surviving tenth-century government record.

First Kings describes Solomon building a temple in Jerusalem, with cedar panelling, carved decoration and gold. It even pictures stones prepared before reaching the building site. These details shaped later religious memory and architectural imagination; quoting the description does not establish that an excavated building is Solomon’s temple.

Archaeologist Kyle Keimer warns that modern labels such as empire can smuggle modern expectations into ancient evidence. He asks how rulers controlled territory and persuaded communities to recognize their authority. Researchers therefore debate both the size of the proposed kingdom and what political unity would actually have meant.

A later discovery provides a different kind of clue. Ninth-century BCE fragments of the Tel Dan stele carry an Aramaic reference to the House of David. Found in 1993 and 1994, they attest that dynastic name outside the Bible. They do not draw David’s borders or establish the scale of his government.

A 2024 Jerusalem study assembled 103 radiocarbon measurements from five excavation areas. Some charred remains dated to the twelfth through tenth centuries BCE. The authors identify early occupation whose character remains uncertain. Tiny organic fragments can establish human presence without telling us whether a particular king ordered a particular wall.

At Khirbet Qeiyafa, researchers dated 17 burnt olive pits found together inside a jar in a destruction layer. Four were divided between two laboratories as a check. The results placed them around 1000 BCE. An olive pit becomes a clock because the carbon it absorbed while growing changes predictably after death.

Qeiyafa’s excavators interpret its fortifications and public buildings as evidence for early Judahite organization. Alexander Fantalkin and Israel Finkelstein instead emphasize northern connections in its material culture. The town is real; its political affiliation and precise chronology remain disputed. A dated town cannot, by itself, settle every argument about a united kingdom.

A large Qeiyafa building occupied the summit, with walls thicker than those of ordinary houses. Excavators call it a probable administrative building. Another building beside the city wall contained rows of stone columns and was interpreted as a storehouse. Organizing storage and substantial construction required coordinated work, whoever held political authority.

Qeiyafa also yielded hundreds of storage jars, with fingerprints pressed into handles. Their clay was locally sourced according to material analysis. Such repeated marks helped archaeologists investigate organized production and storage. Ancient fingerprints are a wonderfully direct trace of hands at work, although they do not identify the individual potters.

sections.title: Cooking, trade and very busy bees

items.text: The excavated Qeiyafa houses included courtyards, several rooms and spaces built into the double city wall. Clay cooking ovens found in courtyards place some food preparation outdoors. A household’s working space could extend into what looks, on a plan, like military architecture: the city wall also helped form people’s back rooms.

Grinding equipment at Qeiyafa came from different landscapes. Some stones were made from coastal beach rock, while basalt tools connected the settlement with other source areas. Cypriot juglets and Egyptian objects add evidence of wider exchange. Even preparing food could depend on materials brought from beyond the immediate neighbourhood.

At Tel Rehov in the Jordan Valley, clay cylinders from the tenth to early ninth centuries BCE proved to be beehives. Researchers found actual bee remains inside them, including immature bees. This is regional evidence for specialist food production around the debated period, without demonstrating that David or Solomon controlled the apiary.

The Tel Rehov bees resembled an Anatolian subspecies rather than the local one. Researchers proposed two possibilities: bee populations once had different ranges, or beekeepers imported suitable colonies. Either way, managing hives inside a town took skill. Honey production involved rather more planning than finding something sweet and hoping it would not sting.

Qeiyafa’s ritual rooms contained special objects, including small shrine models. A carved stone example reproduces elaborate doorways and roof details. These models offer rare evidence for how people represented sacred buildings. Archaeologists compare them with later architectural traditions and biblical descriptions, while keeping the models distinct from the Jerusalem temple itself.

sections.title: Later Judah: writing, people and health

items.text: A securely identified later Hebrew sample appears on royal jar handles from Jerusalem around 700 BCE: l-m-l-k, meaning “belonging to the king”. This is the museum’s Latin-letter transcription of Hebrew letters, not an imitation of their ancient shapes. These administrative stamps belong to later Judah, roughly three centuries after the traditional setting of Solomon.

A jasper seal from Lachish, dated 750-700 BCE, combines a winged sphinx with a Hebrew inscription naming Hannah as its owner. The Ashmolean notes that surviving women’s seals from this period are rare. This later object brings a named woman into view, although it cannot tell us how every family divided property or work.

Later Jerusalem even preserves evidence from the toilet. A study of two latrines, dated to the seventh and early sixth centuries BCE, detected Giardia parasite antigens in both. The result reveals an intestinal-health problem in these households. These are centuries-later Judahite finds, so they cannot diagnose people living in David’s time.

First Kings explains the kingdom’s division through a dispute over heavy labour: Rehoboam refuses demands for relief, and northern Israelites choose Jeroboam. That is the text’s account of political rupture after Solomon. Much later, Babylonian records document Judean families rebuilding livelihoods abroad through farming, contracts and business, showing lives continuing after royal institutions ended.

ending.text: The biblical account describes division after Solomon. Later Israel lost independence to Assyria in the late eighth century BCE, and Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE. Judean communities continued under subsequent empires. Neither conquest matches the imported map’s 500 BCE endpoint.
